Key Achievements • Demonstration of new use case for emergent manufacturing process: Electrospray processing has been used to manufacture nanomaterials and to facilitate separations of macromolecules in mass spectrometry, but it is relatively new to polymer processing. This work establishes a new use case for electrospray- based manufacturing. • Successful synthesis of thin electrocaloric films: Electrospray processing of electroactive materials was demonstrated to create films with electrocaloric properties. These films were some of the thinnest ever derived for electrocaloric purposes. • Evidence of manufacturing-driven benefits: We showed that electrospray likely creates microscopic domains of crystallinity or order that may contribute to 25 DE-EE0009099 enhance temperature lift during electrocaloric cycling. These benefits were demonstrated over traditional casting techniques. • Remarkable diaelectric breakdown strength: Working with exceptionally thin films increases the likelihood of defects or imperfections that can lead to dialectric breakdown. Our films exhibited remarkable strength and resiliency under high electric field conditions. • Challenges with LC blends: Blending LCs with the PVDF terpolymer proved difficult due to phase separation and lack of film stability. • LC Blends showed no improvement in performance: We determined that the LC blends may not be working because the activation temperature (i.e. the temperature at which the LCs will exhibit their electrocaloric behavior) is higher than the PVDF terpolymer. Our testing was done at room temperature while the LCs generally activate at higher temperatures. We were happy to see that the addition of the LCs did not reduce the temperature lift, more tests at higher temperature would be useful. We did not conduct these tests because we ran out of time and funds on the project. • Successful Dissemination of results: This work resulted in one refereed publication in Cell Reports Physical Science (IF 7.3) and 6 conference presentations (Poster and oral) 5. Benefits Assessment With the relatively small project, we did not conduct a full analysis of the benefits of this technology relative to existing HVAC-type systems. When the project started, our partner (RTX, then UTC) still had technology offerings in the HVAC space. Once they spun off Carrier, their interest in that business sector waned. While their interest remained in the technology at large, we never conducted a quantifiable benefits analysis. It is widely accepted that using electrocaloric cooling confers benefits over vapor- compression cooling (efficiency, lack of refrigerants, low noise, potential to miniaturize, reduced maintenance), many of these benefits are still hypothetical due to the challenges that continue to plague the space. High electric fields require power electronics that are expensive. Electrical breakdown and degradation under high electric fields is a challenge. Even with the higher efficiency, temperature lifts are still low compared to vapor compression systems and overall heat removal capacity, particularly for thin films, can be limited. A more expansive study with a techno-economic assessment is recommended to explore these tradeoffs more thoroughly. 6.
